attempts.label: CRCNS:ac-1
attempts.entry_title: Long-lasting context dependence in rat auditory cortex (Asari & Zador 2009)
attempts.summary: The paper's central finding held in this data: A1 responses depend on the preceding sound for seconds, the context-dependent power decaying with a time constant of about 1 s as reported, while in the thalamus (MGB) the effect fades fast. Fewer probes showed significant context dependence than reported, the bound on short-window models rose more slowly, and longer STRF windows did improve predictions, under a fold averaging the paper does not describe. Amplitude and frequency changes outlasted modulation and higher-order changes, but the proportions did not match, on stimulus groupings rebuilt because the paper does not list them. The synaptic conductance findings could not be tested, as the data set holds no voltage-clamp recordings.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Asari and Zador (2009) on CRCNS ac-1, which holds the whole-cell recordings of 39 A1 neurons tested with natural sounds, 96 A1 neurons tested with synthetic sound ensembles and the cell-attached recordings of 14 MGB neurons, with the authors' analysis scripts. It measures how long the response to a probe sound depends on the preceding sound, by a pointwise Kruskal-Wallis test and by the context-dependent fraction of the response power, the role of single sound properties, and the fast decay in thalamus. The voltage-clamp recordings are not in the data set.

outcomes.statement: Of 194 A1 cells recorded in current clamp, 123 met the analysis criterion (39 tested with natural sounds, 14 with TORCs, 6 with DMRs, 39 with modulated harmonic tones, 27 with modulated colored noise); 14 of 42 voltage-clamped cells and 14 of 16 MGB cells were analysed.
outcomes.source: Methods, Electrophysiology, paragraphs 2 and 3; Table 1
outcomes.quote: All together, we recorded from 194 cells in 139 animals in current-clamp mode, of which 123 cells met our criterion for the analysis ... Of these, 39 cells were examined with natural sound ensembles, 14 cells with ensembles of temporally orthogonal ripple combinations, 6 cells with ensembles of dynamic moving ripples, 39 cells with ensembles of modulated harmonic tones, and 27 cells with ensembles of modulated colored noise ensembles
outcomes.notes: Natural-sound A1 probes 305 in 39 cells (paper 305, 39) under both readings of silence, as every probe has at least two non-silent contexts. MGB probes 93 in 14 cells (paper 93, 14); the data set holds 14 MGB cells, the paper recorded 16. A1 current-clamp cells meeting the criterion 132 (39 natural, 95 synthetic, 2 in both) against 123; one synthetic-sound cell (20061231-ha2-001) has no eligible probe. By the families of their recordings the 132 cells are 37 natural only, 26 MHT, 26 MCN, 14 DMR, 14 natural-sound variants, 13 TORC, one natural and TORC and one natural and DMR (the notebook lists them); by stimulus family the cells with an eligible ensemble are TORC 14 (paper 14), DMR 15 (6), MHT 26 (39), MCN 26 (27) and natural-sound variants 14, so the families do not map onto the paper's and the 9 cells that make the difference cannot be named. The voltage-clamp counts (29 probes, 14 cells) cannot be tested: the data set holds no voltage-clamp recording. No measured values are recorded, as the record needs one number for each of the seven expected values and two were not measured; the five measured counts are 132, 39, 305, 93 and 14. The TORC, DMR, MHT and MCN probe counts by property are reported under fig8a-proportion-by-property.
deviations: Details the Methods leave open are taken from the authors' scripts shipped in the data set (asari/Tools/CxtDep.m, ViewResp.m, GetEvoked.m), which the paper does not link: probes are the fragments' stated durations, a fragment at the start of a sequence has silence (the preceding 4 s) as context, trials of one context are pooled and every context is cut to the smallest trial count, the Kruskal-Wallis test uses ordinal ranks without a tie correction, and each trial is centred on its mean over the probe window for the power measures.
In 20051108-ha1-001 (A1) and 20071010-ha2-005 (MGB) the stored fragment lists of the cell's two files are swapped; each file's probes are cut with the list that fits its triggers.
The cells per stimulus family are counted by the trigger type of each recording, which need not be how the paper assigned a cell to an ensemble type.

outcomes.statement: Firing rates were low in A1 (spontaneous 0.47 +/- 0.61 Hz, evoked 0.57 +/- 0.77 Hz, mean +/- SD, 194 cells) and high in MGB (spontaneous 0.78 +/- 1.25 Hz, evoked 11.4 +/- 16.9 Hz, 16 cells).
outcomes.source: Methods, Analysis, paragraphs 2 and 3; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 1; Results, Subcortical contribution to context dependence, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Because of the low firing rates in A1 (spontaneous, 0.47 ... 0.61 Hz; evoked, 0.57 ... 0.77 Hz ... 194 cells ... Sufficiently high firing rates in MGB allowed us to analyze the context dependence at the spike level (spontaneous, 0.78 ... 1.25 Hz; evoked, 11.4 ... 16.9 Hz
outcomes.notes: Main reading (A1 spikes at -20 mV, MGB spikes by the authors' GetSpikes.m automatic detector; spontaneous over the whole intersequence silence; evoked over all sound periods). A1, 133 cells (39 natural, 96 synthetic, 2 in both): spontaneous 0.392 +/- 0.614 Hz, evoked 0.439 +/- 0.689 Hz (paper 0.47 +/- 0.61, 0.57 +/- 0.77, 194 cells). MGB, 14 cells: spontaneous 0.549 +/- 1.236 Hz, evoked 4.99 +/- 11.45 Hz (paper 0.78 +/- 1.25, 11.4 +/- 16.9, 16 cells). The last 1 s before each sequence gives 0.415 (A1) and 0.709 Hz (MGB, within 10%). No reading has all four means within 10%. The A1 means are below 1 Hz at every threshold (-10 mV 0.228 and 0.248 Hz, -30 mV 0.601 and 0.669 Hz). The MGB evoked mean is above 5 Hz with robust thresholds on the same filter, 13.57 Hz at 5 SD and 10.38 Hz at 8 SD (within tolerance; spontaneous 1.66 and 0.975 Hz), so the partial rule holds under those readings; with the authors' detector it is 4.99 Hz, just under 5 Hz. The criterion asks for a standard detector on each reading, so the outcome is partial. Before round 1 it was recorded as not reproduced, on the authors' detector alone; the verifier gave partial. The outcome rests on the detectors. Question for the authors: how were A1 spikes detected and with what threshold, and which periods were taken as spontaneous and evoked?
deviations: A1 spikes are upward crossings of -20 mV on the raw membrane potential with a 2-ms dead time (assumed; the paper does not say how A1 spikes were found, and GetSpikes.m extracts them by hand in whole-cell mode). -10 and -30 mV are shown.

MGB spikes use the authors' GetSpikes.m automatic mode (FIR high-pass forward and backward, threshold at 2/3 of the largest filtered value, spike at the peak), which matches the Methods' "high-pass filter and thresholding", and robust thresholds of 5 and 8 SD on the same filter (assumed; the paper gives no threshold). The outcome is partial under the robust thresholds and would fail the partial rule by 0.01 Hz under the authors' detector.
The data set holds 133 of the 194 A1 cells and 14 of the 16 MGB cells the paper averages over.

outcomes.statement: The example A1 neuron of Figure 2 had high trial-to-trial reliability (correlation across trials 0.74 +/- 0.08 for the shown probe and 0.61 +/- 0.07 over the seven natural sound fragments tested), and the mean correlation over the population was 0.31 +/- 0.09.
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence, paragraph 2; Figure 2A legend
outcomes.quote: the correlation coefficient of the response traces across trials in a given context was 0.61 ... 0.07 (mean ... SD) for the seven natural sound fragments tested in this cell. The reliability varied within a given neuron as a function of the stimuli tested and across neurons; the mean correlation coefficient was 0.31 ... 0.09
outcomes.notes: Mean pairwise correlation of trials within a context, over the probe window, averaged over contexts: 0.310 +/- 0.092 over 39 cells (paper 0.31 +/- 0.09), 0.319 +/- 0.129 over 305 probes. The cell 20051222-ha1-001 (seven fragments, six repeats) has 0.611 +/- 0.081 over its seven probes (paper 0.61 +/- 0.07) and 0.737 for probe 4 (paper 0.74 +/- 0.08), heard after silence and two fragments, as in Figure 2B. The four other cells with seven fragments and six repeats have 0.244 to 0.309. The leave-one-out reading gives 0.437 over cells.

outcomes.statement: In an example A1 neuron, changing the conditioning stimulus changed the response to the probe for about 4 s; responses did not differ between 2 and 4 s after probe onset and diverged again after about 4 s.
outcomes.source: Figure 2A legend, Figure 2B and 2D; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, context-induced differences could sometimes be intermittent; the three average response traces showed no difference in the interval 2 to 4 s after the onset of the probe, but diverged again after about 4 s

statistics.test: Kruskal-Wallis test at each time point, P < 0.01 for at least 5 ms
statistics.n: one cell, one probe in three contexts (6 repeats shown for one context in Figure 2A)

outcomes.notes: Tested on the claim as amended after a reader's answer (questions/asari-2009.yaml, answered 2026-11-15). The answer changed two things. The example is now the probe of the cell that matches the Figure 2 reliabilities within 10% (no longer any of the candidates), and the windows carry the 10% tolerance (significant before 2 s, none between 2.2 and 3.6 s, one starting after 3.6 s). Of 40 probes in seven-fragment cells heard after silence and two fragments with six or more trials, one matches: 20051222-ha1-001 probe 4 (contexts silence, fragments 2 and 3, six trials each), cell 0.611 +/- 0.081 over its seven probes (0.61 +/- 0.07), probe 0.737 +/- 0.075 (0.74 +/- 0.08). Its significant periods run to 1.60 s, none falls between 1.60 and 3.97 s, and they resume from 3.97 to 4.60 s, so the amended pattern holds. Before the answer the outcome was also reproduced, on the same probe, but only by reading the run that starts at 3.970 s as the divergence after about 4 s; under the strict 2 to 4 s window it overlaps by 30 ms. The amended windows now settle this without that reading. No probe matches in the leave-one-out reading (cell 0.732) or when the cell SD must also be within 10% of 0.07 (0.081); the claim would not be testable under those readings. For reference, 3 of the 40 probes meet the amended windows and 2 the strict ones; 15 of 305 natural-sound probes have a significant period later than 4 s.
deviations: Details the Methods leave open are taken from the authors' scripts shipped in the data set (asari/Tools/CxtDep.m, ViewResp.m, GetEvoked.m), which the paper does not link: probes are the fragments' stated durations, a fragment at the start of a sequence has silence (the preceding 4 s) as context, trials of one context are pooled and every context is cut to the smallest trial count, the Kruskal-Wallis test uses ordinal ranks without a tie correction, and each trial is centred on its mean over the probe window for the power measures.

Assumed: the match is made on the two mean correlations (cell over its fragments, and probe), the values the criterion means by "the closest to both", in the pairwise reading, which is the one that reproduces the population value of fig2-example-reliability (0.310 against 0.31; leave-one-out gives 0.437). The SDs are reported but not matched: an SD over seven fragments is too uncertain to be held to 10%, and the cell SD (0.081 against 0.07) is the only value that misses.
The probe's SD (0.075) is the SD of the pairwise trial correlations pooled over its three contexts; the paper does not say over what the 0.08 is taken (Figure 2A legend).

outcomes.statement: Of 305 natural sound probes tested in 39 A1 cells with typically five to eight natural sound contexts, 204 (66.9%) showed significant context dependence, and about a quarter (23.7%) of the significant events occurred more than 1 s after probe onset.
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence, paragraph 6; Figure 3A
outcomes.quote: Of 305 natural sound probe stimuli tested with different ... typically around five to eight ... natural sound contexts in 39 cells, significant effects were observed in 204 probes (66.9%; Fig. 3A), and about a quarter (23.7%) of the events occurred longer than one second after the onset of a probe stimulus
outcomes.notes: Silence counted as a context: 183 of 305 probes significant (60.0%) against 204 (66.9%); the count is 21 below (tolerance 20.4) and the fraction 0.002 below its lower bound of 0.602. Late fraction (1 minus the noise-corrected cumulative probability at 1 s) 0.225 over all 305 probes and 0.237 over running probes (paper 0.237), with the cumulative curve peaking at 4.718 s (paper 4.72 s). Silence left out: 160 significant (52.5%), late fraction 0.139 to 0.144. 35 of 39 cells have a significant probe. The criterion's partial rule needs the count within tolerance, so it does not apply and the outcome is not reproduced (changed from partial after round 1, as the verifier gave); the effect is present but weaker, with its timing reproduced. The Kruskal-Wallis ranks follow CxtDep.m (ordinal, no tie correction; printed in the data check); the traces are stored in int16 steps of 0.0061 to 0.0153 mV, 231 or more steps per trial SD in 95% of probes, so ties are rare.
deviations: Details the Methods leave open are taken from the authors' scripts shipped in the data set (asari/Tools/CxtDep.m, ViewResp.m, GetEvoked.m), which the paper does not link: probes are the fragments' stated durations, a fragment at the start of a sequence has silence (the preceding 4 s) as context, trials of one context are pooled and every context is cut to the smallest trial count, the Kruskal-Wallis test uses ordinal ranks without a tie correction, and each trial is centred on its mean over the probe window for the power measures.
In 20051108-ha1-001 (A1) and 20071010-ha2-005 (MGB) the stored fragment lists of the cell's two files are swapped; each file's probes are cut with the list that fits its triggers.
Proportion curves are stored as 1-ms means of the 0.1-ms significance traces (a standard choice for storage that cannot change the counts).

outcomes.statement: The proportion of probes with significant context dependence decays after probe onset as the sum of two exponentials (sizes 0.17 and 0.09, decay constants 0.20 and 0.90 s), above a noise floor of about 2.8 x 10^-3.
outcomes.source: Figure 3A legend, bottom panel; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.inferred: The fit values are in the Figure 3A legend, where the symbols are garbled in the text extraction (read as alpha1 = 0.17, tau1 = 0.20 s, alpha2 = 0.09, tau2 = 0.90 s, kappa = mean noise floor = 2.8 x 10^-3); the Results restate the long constant as about one second.
outcomes.notes: Constant fixed at the mean noise floor over 0 to 6 s (0.0022 over all probes, 0.0028 over running probes; paper 2.8 x 10^-3). With non-negative sizes, two exponentials are chosen in all four readings with silence counted: fast size 0.146 to 0.154 (paper 0.17; within tolerance in one reading), fast constant 0.253 to 0.265 s (0.20), slow size 0.070 to 0.080 (0.09), slow constant 0.902 to 0.968 s (0.90, within tolerance in all four). Without bounds the fits take a negative fast component that models the rise of the curve in the first 50 ms: with silence counted -0.173 to -0.175 with 0.015 s and a slow constant of 0.42 s, with silence left out -0.200 to -0.204 with 0.022 s and a slow constant of 0.22 s; those readings meet neither rule. Silence left out: one exponential is chosen with non-negative sizes. The outcome rests on the bounds. Question for the authors: were the decay sizes bounded at zero, and from what time was the curve fitted?
deviations: Details the Methods leave open are taken from the authors' scripts shipped in the data set (asari/Tools/CxtDep.m, ViewResp.m, GetEvoked.m), which the paper does not link: probes are the fragments' stated durations, a fragment at the start of a sequence has silence (the preceding 4 s) as context, trials of one context are pooled and every context is cut to the smallest trial count, the Kruskal-Wallis test uses ordinal ranks without a tie correction, and each trial is centred on its mean over the probe window for the power measures.
Exponential fits use scipy.optimize.least_squares with a grid of start values for the time constants (0.02 to 4 s), the analogue of lsqcurvefit; the paper gives no start values or bounds.

Assumed: decay sizes kept non-negative. Eq. 44 calls them decay sizes and the paper's fit has two positive sizes; without bounds the fit uses a negative size for the rise after onset, which is not a decay. Both are shown.

outcomes.statement: The context-dependent fraction of the stimulus-related response power, normalized by the smoothed stimulus-related power, decays from about 0.49 with a time constant of about 1.04 s.
outcomes.source: Figure 3B legend, bottom panel; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: For both measures there was a long decay constant of about one second
outcomes.notes: Q(t) with silence as a context: size 0.487 to 0.495 and constant 1.008 to 1.050 s over the four readings of the average (probes running, all) and fit range (0 to 4 s, 0 to 6 s), all within tolerance (paper 0.49, 1.04 s). Silence left out: 0.553 to 0.555 and 0.545 to 0.549 s, outside. With the two files of 20051108-ha1-001 cut by their stored, swapped fragment lists (data check), the fits with silence counted give 0.464 to 0.468 and 1.74 to 1.78 s, outside tolerance; the result depends on cutting those probes at the right times.

In 20051108-ha1-001 (A1) and 20071010-ha2-005 (MGB) the stored fragment lists of the cell's two files are swapped; each file's probes are cut with the list that fits its triggers.

Assumed: silence counts as a context. The readings differ on it; the authors' CxtDep.m includes the silence before each sequence as a context, Figure 1A lists silence among the contexts and Figure 2B uses it, so it is the best-supported reading.
The running mean over [0, 2t] is cut at the end of the data where 2t passes it (Figure 3B shows the smoothed curve to 6 s).

outcomes.statement: The trial-to-trial noise autocorrelation and the autocorrelation of spontaneous activity decay within about 100 ms, much faster than the second-long timescale of context dependence in A1.
outcomes.source: Methods, Analysis, Timescale of intrinsic membrane properties; Results, Context dependence, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: we found that ... had a sharp peak with a rapid decay (within ... 100 ms; data not shown), much faster than the slow timescale identified in neural responses in area A1
outcomes.notes: Noise autocorrelation (residuals from the context mean, Eq. 14 and 45, averaged over trials of the 305 probes): below 1/e at 71 ms, below 0.1 at 115 ms. Spontaneous activity (intersequence silences of the 46 natural-sound files): 77 and 121 ms, or 75 and 118 ms without the first second. All under 150 ms; the 1/e lags are under 347 ms (a third of 1.04 s).
deviations: Details the Methods leave open are taken from the authors' scripts shipped in the data set (asari/Tools/CxtDep.m, ViewResp.m, GetEvoked.m), which the paper does not link: probes are the fragments' stated durations, a fragment at the start of a sequence has silence (the preceding 4 s) as context, trials of one context are pooled and every context is cut to the smallest trial count, the Kruskal-Wallis test uses ordinal ranks without a tie correction, and each trial is centred on its mean over the probe window for the power measures.

outcomes.statement: Without knowledge of the context, no model can capture more than about half (0.51) of the predictable response power with a window of about 100 ms; the upper bound approaches one only with a window of seconds (time constant 1.04 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Relation to response predictability, paragraph 4; Figure 4 legend
outcomes.quote: shows that no model can capture more than a half
outcomes.notes: Eq. 43 with silence counted: 1 + alpha1 0.445 to 0.496 with the smoothed denominator and 0.495 to 0.502 unsmoothed (paper 0.51, tolerance 0.051); time constants 1.70 to 2.33 s smoothed and 1.20 to 1.24 s unsmoothed (paper 1.04, tolerance 0.104); the smoothed fits over all probes to 6 s run to the 100-s bound. Silence left out: 1.26 to 1.59 s smoothed and 0.70 s unsmoothed. No reading has both values within tolerance and the criterion gives no partial rule, so the outcome is not reproduced (changed from partial after round 1, as the verifier gave). The fitted bound near onset is about half (1 + alpha1 0.445 to 0.502), and the approach to one takes seconds, slower than the paper's constant. The mean over the first 100 ms is 0.570 for the smoothed ratio and 0.453 unsmoothed with silence counted, 0.655 and 0.509 without it. Variant, not a reading of the criterion: 1 - Q(t) with silence counted gives 1 + alpha1 0.505 to 0.513 and time constants 1.008 to 1.050 s, within tolerance; the Figure 4 legend gives the same fit as Figure 3B. Whether Figure 4 plots 1 - Q is asked in questions/asari-2009.yaml.

outcomes.statement: Linear STRF models of 20 A1 cells from Machens et al. (2004) predicted less than about 20% of the predictable response power, and extending the window from 180 ms to about 4 s did not improve them significantly, with or without a static nonlinearity; the LN model did only slightly better.
outcomes.source: Results, Relation to response predictability, paragraph 5; Figure 4; Discussion, Context dependence and model construction, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: The performance of STRF-based models was in general unsatisfactory ... consistent with previous work (Ahrens et al. 2008; Machens et al. 2004; Sahani and Linden 2003). The performance did not improve significantly, however, when we extended the window length
outcomes.notes: Tested after round 1 (the verifier found it testable). Validation performance pooled over the folds, mean over the 16 Wehr cells with natural sounds heard at least twice (main reading): STRF 0.163 at 180 ms rising to 0.196 at 4052 ms (largest mean 0.198 at 1364 ms), LN 0.127 to 0.145 (largest 0.171). In every pooled reading (20-ms spectrogram window, folds by stimulus, each window scored on its own samples, all 25 cells) the means stay at or below 0.208 for STRF and 0.191 for LN, under 0.22, but the one-sided Wilcoxon test finds an improvement of the STRF from 180 to 4052 ms (p 0.000 to 0.042; median gain 0.024 per cell in the main reading), while LN shows none (p 0.106 to 0.450). LN does worse than the STRF on average (-0.043), not slightly better. Training (upper) means reach 0.29 to 0.50, so the 20% fits the validation estimate. The criterion is met in one combination, folds by stimulus with validation averaged over folds as STRFanalysis.m averages it (STRF at most 0.129, Wilcoxon p 0.202; LN p 0.450); with the code's contiguous folds the fold average reaches means of 0.59 to 0.86 for STRF, as a fold of a stimulus heard twice can hold little predictable power. The outcome rests on pooling over folds. The chosen ridge value is inside the grid in all 675 fits. Question for the authors: which 20 cells were used, and was the validation performance averaged over folds or computed over the pooled validation data?
deviations: Method from the Methods (Neural encoding models, Model performance) and the authors' wehr/Tools/STRFanalysis.m, ridgesvd1.m, logspectrogram.m and ViewResponse.m, reimplemented in wehr_strf.py: 17 frequency bins at 3 per octave from 0.40 kHz, 45 pseudo-logarithmic time bins as listed (windows 180 to 4052 ms), Hann spectrogram window of 10 or 20 ms, 4-ms response bins of the 10-ms median-filtered membrane potential, ridge regression on the trial mean with 10-fold cross-validation, robust lowess (5% span, 5 iterations) for the static nonlinearity, Eq. 53 for the performance.

Assumed: the cells. The paper reanalysed 20 of Wehr's cells without naming them; the data set holds 25, of which 16 have stimuli heard at least twice. The 16 (repeated stimuli only) are the main reading; all 25, with STRFanalysis.m's rule that a stimulus heard once has half its total power as predictable power, are the other.

Assumed: validation performance computed over the pooled validation data (Eq. 53 averages over time), with the ridge value chosen on it; the mean over folds of per-fold values (STRFanalysis.m) is shown as a variant and is the only reading under which the criterion is met (with folds by stimulus).

Every window is scored on the same response bins, those at least 4052 ms after stimulus onset (main); scoring each window on its own samples (STRFanalysis.m drops the window length) is a variant. The ridge grid is 1e-3 to 1e4 times the mean eigenvalue of S'S (a standard choice).

The main reading departs from the authors' STRFanalysis.m in two places, pooling the validation data over folds where the code averages per-fold values, and scoring every window on the same samples where the code scores each on its own. The code's choices are run as variants. The one combination that meets the criterion (folds by stimulus, fold average) is not taken as the main reading because it gives the LN model a negative validation performance at every window (mean -0.112 to -0.198, strf cell 6), which does not fit Figure 4, where LN does slightly better than the STRF; with the code's contiguous folds the fold average fails the criterion (STRF means up to 0.83 and 0.86).
The test of "did not improve significantly" (one-sided paired Wilcoxon, 4052 against 180 ms, at 0.05) is the claims file's; the outcome rests on it.

outcomes.statement: In an example voltage-clamped A1 cell, excitatory and inhibitory conductances evoked by the probe decayed within about 100 ms in all six contexts, yet their variance over contexts lasted long, longer for inhibition than for excitation.
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence of synaptic conductances, paragraph 2; Figure 5D to 5G
outcomes.quote: In all cases we examined, both excitatory and inhibitory conductances elicited in this cell decayed rapidly within about 100 ms, yet the context dependence measured as the variance of the conductances lasted long, especially for the inhibitory conductance in this example
outcomes.notes: The data set holds no voltage-clamp recording: every A1 recording read is whole-cell current clamp and every MGB recording cell-attached, and Summary.mat lists no voltage-clamp experiment. The files not analysed, the 15 of the unpublished experiment and the 161 tuning curves, are also whole-cell or cell-attached recordings in mV, and Wehr's natural-sound recordings are whole-cell. The paper recorded 42 cells in voltage clamp.

outcomes.statement: Across 29 probes in 14 voltage-clamped cells, context dependence of both excitatory and inhibitory conductances decayed with a long constant of seconds (1.22 and 2.50 s) and a short one of hundreds of milliseconds (0.14 and 0.13 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Context dependence of synaptic conductances, paragraph 3; Figure 6A and 6B
outcomes.quote: For both excitatory and inhibitory conductances, there was a long decay constant on the order of seconds
outcomes.notes: The data set holds no voltage-clamp recording (recording types of all 172 files read: 151 whole-cell current clamp, 21 cell-attached; the 15 files of the unpublished experiment and the 161 tuning curves are whole-cell or cell-attached with traces in mV).

outcomes.statement: When only one property of synthetic conditioning stimuli varied, context dependence was found in 77 of 95 probes (81.1%, 31 cells) for amplitude, 73 of 110 (35 cells) for frequency, 62 of 96 (64.6%, 27 cells) for AM, 47 of 82 (57.3%, 25 cells) for FM and 59 of 137 (43.1%, 27 cells) for higher-order properties.
outcomes.source: Results, Relation to stimulus properties, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 8A
outcomes.quote: we observed context-dependent effects in 77 probes (81.1%) of 95 probes (tested in 31 cells) and in 73/110 (64.6%; 35 cells), respectively (Fig. 8A) ... Context-dependent effects were observed in 62/96 (64.6%; 27 cells) for AM modulation; in 47/82 (57.3%; 25 cells) for FM modulation; and in 59/137 (43.1%; 27 cells) for colored noise modulation
outcomes.notes: Table 1 reading, which the claims file asks for (the populations follow the columns of Table 1): probes for amplitude, frequency and higher-order, probe x ensemble entries for AM and FM, the counts that give Table 1's denominators 95, 110, 96 and 82 and the MHT sub-rows 71 and 57 (the measured values). Amplitude 58/95 (paper 77/95), frequency 62/110 (73/110), AM 41/96 (62/96), FM 29/82 (47/82), higher-order 64/131 (59/137); only higher-order is within tolerance. Amplitude > frequency holds (0.611 > 0.564), but AM > FM > higher-order fails: AM (0.427) and FM (0.354) both fall below higher-order (0.489), so the partial rule does not hold. findings.statement: The data set holds no voltage-clamp recording. The paper recorded 42 A1 cells in voltage clamp and analysed 14 (29 probes, Figures 5 and 6); every A1 file is a current-clamp whole-cell recording, including the unpublished experiment and the tuning curves (traces in mV), and Summary.mat lists no voltage-clamp experiment, so the conductance findings cannot be tested.

In two cells the fragment lists (param.stimulus) of the cell's two recordings are swapped: 20051108-ha1-001-002 and -003 (A1) and 20071010-ha2-005-002 and -003 (MGB). The stored fragment durations of each file add up to the other file's sequence trigger durations to within 0.2 ms and miss its own by up to 1.8 s (A1) and 2.3 s (MGB). Cut with the stored lists, the probes of these files start at the wrong times; the fit of Figure 3B changes from 0.46 to 0.47 and 1.74 to 1.78 s to 0.49 and 1.01 to 1.05 s when they are corrected.

In 20061201-ha2-001-002 every sequence trigger is 308 ms longer than the sum of its seven stored fragment durations (4200 ms each), and no other file of the cell fits. The true fragment boundaries are unknown; the stored durations were used, as the authors' CxtDep.m would use them.
20061231-ha2-001-002 states 4 effective repeats, but one of its sequences is presented 3 times.

Five TORC recordings described as bandwidth variants (20060313-ha1-001, 20060313-ha1-002, 20060314-ha1-001, 20060315-ha1-001, 20060315-ha1-002) store no frequency band for their fragments, and their stimulus parameters are identical, so the variants can be told apart only by their description.

The data set does not say which cells the paper used. The A1 synthetic-sound group holds 96 cells, of which 95 meet the paper's inclusion rule, so with the 39 natural-sound cells 132 A1 cells meet it against the paper's 123, and the cells per stimulus family (TORC 14, DMR 15, MHT 26, MCN 26, natural-sound variants 14) do not map onto the paper's (14, 6, 39, 27). The 25 cells of Wehr's data include the 20 the paper reanalysed, which are not named.
The recording of Figure 7 (a natural probe after DMR contexts in the bands 0.625-2.5, 2.5-10 and 10-40 kHz) is not in the data set; no DMR recording stores those bands.

Summary.mat lists two cells, 20060314-ha1-001 and 20060320-ha3-003, in both the natural-sound group and the synthetic-sound group, and lists their tuning-curve file (-001) under each, so a count over the groups counts these cells and files twice. Their sequence recordings differ between the groups (natural -004 and -003; synthetic -002 and -003, and -002).

The claims file says the populations follow the Table 1 columns. Under that reading the order fails: AM 41/96 (0.427) and FM 29/82 (0.354) both fall below higher-order 64/131 (0.489). Only the higher-order count is within tolerance, so the outcome is not reproduced. The partial outcome holds only under the uniform readings, whose denominators do not match Table 1. The Table 1 legend says each row is a probe type; counting further ensembles of natural probes as the MHT row conflicts with that, so the question to the authors stands. The record should report this reading, and its deviation text, which cites the denominators as support for the reading it says it dropped, should be corrected.

verifications.reviewed: Round 3. Only the one change of outcome proposed after round 2 (fig8a-proportion-by-property), with the re-executed notebook, the claims file and the paper. Report in transcripts/asari-2009/verifier-3-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The paper does not say how A1 spikes were detected or which periods count as spontaneous and evoked for the firing rates (Methods, Analysis, paragraph 2); the authors' GetSpikes.m extracts whole-cell spikes by hand. This attempt used a -20 mV threshold. Question for the authors: what detector and threshold, and which windows, give 0.47 and 0.57 Hz?

The exponential fits (Eq. 44) give no bounds, start values or fit range. On these data an unbounded two-exponential fit of the Figure 3A curve takes a negative fast size for the rise in the first 50 ms; with sizes bounded at zero it gives slow constants of 0.90 to 0.97 s. Question for the authors: were the sizes bounded at zero, and over which times were the curves fitted?

Table 1 and Figure 8 do not say which conditioning stimuli form each property's ensemble, nor whether a probe tested with several ensembles of one property (for example AM variants at four FM settings) counts once or once per ensemble. The stored parameters reproduce the denominators for amplitude and frequency only when probes are counted and for AM and FM only when ensembles are counted. The split by probe type does not match Table 1: the data set holds 14 MHT probes with property ensembles (AM, 2 cells) against the MHT row of 25, 25, 71 and 57, while the further AM and FM ensembles of the 25 natural probes plus those 14 entries number exactly 71 and 57. Question for the authors: how were the ensembles formed and counted, and are the MHT counts of Table 1 further ensembles of natural probes?

The Methods do not say whether silence counts among the contexts of Figures 3 and 4. The authors' CxtDep.m, shipped with the data, includes the preceding intersequence silence as a context; the Figure 3B fit is reproduced with it (1.01 to 1.05 s) and not without it (0.55 s). Question for the authors: was silence a context in Figures 3 and 4, as the script does?

The paper does not name the recording of Figure 2. The data set has one probe whose reliabilities match the legend (20051222-ha1-001-002, probe 4, 0.611 +/- 0.081 and 0.737), matched on the mean correlations; its cell SD is 0.081 against 0.07. Question for the authors: is this the Figure 2 example, and is the correlation the mean over pairs of trials?

The STRF analysis (Figure 4) used 20 of Wehr's cells, which the paper does not name; the data set holds 25, 16 of them with stimuli heard at least twice. The paper does not say whether the validation performance (Eq. 53) is computed over the pooled validation data or averaged over folds, as STRFanalysis.m does; with 10 contiguous folds the fold average is unstable (means up to 0.86) and with pooled data the STRF improves significantly from 180 to 4052 ms (Wilcoxon p 0.001, 16 cells). Question for the authors: which cells, and which average?

The Figure 4 legend gives the fit of Eq. 43 as alpha1 = -0.49 and tau1 = 1.04 s, the size and time constant of the Figure 3B fit of Q(t). Eq. 43 equals 1 - Q(t) only where the stimulus-related power equals its running mean over [0, 2t], which it does not here (0.67 to 0.80 of it at 0.5 to 4 s); Eq. 43 gives time constants of 1.2 to 2.3 s and 1 - Q gives 1.01 to 1.05 s. Question for the authors: does Figure 4 plot Eq. 43 or 1 - Q(t)?
The Results give 73/110 frequency probes as 64.6%; 73/110 is 66.4%, and 64.6% is the AM figure (62/96).

Probes last 1.98 to 6.06 s (of the 305 natural-sound probes, 304 still run at 2 s, 214 at 4 s and 24 at 6 s), and the paper does not say how the population curves of Figures 3, 4, 8 and 9D treat times after a probe has ended. The late fraction of Figure 3A is 0.225 with ended probes counted as not significant and 0.237 over the probes still running (paper 0.237). Question for the authors: is the average at time t over all probes, an ended probe counting as zero, or over the probes still running?

The authors' CxtDep.m (FracPow, line 346) centres each trial on its own mean over the probe window before computing the fractional powers, with a whole-trace centring commented out (line 347); the Methods (Analysis, paragraph 1) centre the response over time without saying over which window. This attempt follows the script.

entries.name: asari-2009
entries.title: Long-lasting context dependence in rat auditory cortex (Asari & Zador 2009)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Asari and Zador (2009) on CRCNS ac-1, which holds the whole-cell recordings of 39 A1 neurons tested with natural sounds, 96 A1 neurons tested with synthetic sound ensembles and the cell-attached recordings of 14 MGB neurons, with the authors' analysis scripts. It measures how long the response to a probe sound depends on the preceding sound, by a pointwise Kruskal-Wallis test and by the context-dependent fraction of the response power, the role of single sound properties, and the fast decay in thalamus. The voltage-clamp recordings are not in the data set.
